plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two panels, (a) and (b), illustrating the limiting definition of a tangent line. Panel (a): a smooth curve in the xy-plane with a fixed point P and a moveable point Q marked on the curve; multiple pink secant lines through P fan outward, converging toward a limiting position labeled Tangent line, with arrows indicating the rotational approach to the limit. Panel (b): the same construction applied to a circle, showing P and Q on the circle with multiple secant lines rotating toward the tangent line at P. The figure establishes the general definition of a tangent line as the limiting position of secant lines as Q approaches P along the curve, and confirms that this definition agrees with the classical tangent to a circle.

interactionPlan.concept: The tangent line at a point P on a curve is the limiting position of the secant lines through P and a second point Q as Q approaches P along the curve — a definition that works both for general curves and for circles.
elements: x-axis and y-axis with arrowheads, labeled x and y (panel a only)
smooth blue open curve (gentle S-shape) in panel (a)
blue circle in panel (b)
fixed point P on the curve (blue dot, labeled P)
moveable point Q on the curve (blue dot, labeled Q)
pink secant line through P and Q, labeled 'Secant line'
faint gray/pink ghosted intermediate secant lines fanning out from P, showing prior positions of Q
limiting pink tangent line through P, labeled 'Tangent line'
curved gray arrow showing the secant line rotating toward the tangent position
shaded pink wedge between the current secant and the tangent line (shrinks as Q → P)
live slope readout label: 'slope of secant = m' near the secant line
panel labels (a) and (b)

interactions.teaches: As Q slides along the curve toward P, the secant line through P and Q rotates and its slope settles to a single limiting value — that limiting line is the tangent at P

interactions.label: Curve
interactions.teaches: The same secant-line limiting process defines the tangent on any smooth curve, and on a circle it reproduces the familiar perpendicular-to-radius tangent — so the limit definition generalizes the classical one
Moving P along the curve changes the limiting slope — the tangent direction depends on the point of tangency, which is the seed of the derivative as a function of position

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A tangent line is not defined by 'touching at one point' but by a limit: it is the unique line the secants through P and Q approach as Q → P, and this single definition works for every smooth curve, including the circle.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two-panel figure, but show one panel at a time per the toggle. Panel (a): axes at left/bottom, blue S-shaped curve rising to a rounded crest then falling; P at a lower-left point on the curve, Q farther along near the crest. Panel (b): a large blue circle with P on the upper-left arc and Q on the upper-right arc. In both panels draw: one live pink secant through P and Q (extend beyond both), 3-4 faint ghosted secants fanning from P toward steeper positions, a bold steep pink tangent through P at the top of the fan, a translucent pink wedge between live secant and tangent, and a curved gray arrow near the top pointing from the secant fan toward the tangent. Labels: 'Secant line' to the right of the shallowest line, 'Tangent line' upper left of the steep line, italic P and Q beside their dots. The live secant, wedge, and slope readout must update continuously while dragging Q; ghost lines and tangent stay fixed for a given P. Slope readout shows the numeric secant slope converging to the tangent slope value as Q nears P.

authoredInteractions:
- Drag point Q along the curve toward fixed point P and watch the secant line rotate to become the tangent line, with the slope value updating in real time

authoredContext: To obtain a definition of a tangent line that applies to curves other than circles, we must view tangent lines another way. For this purpose, suppose that we are interested in the tangent line at a point P on a curve in the xy-plane and that Q is any point that lies on the curve and is different from P. The line through P and Q is called a secant line for the curve at P. Intuition suggests that if we move the point Q along the curve toward P, then the secant line will rotate toward a limiting position. The line in this limiting position is what we will consider to be the tangent line at P (Figure 1.1.4a). As suggested by Figure 1.1.4b, this new concept of a tangent line coincides with the traditional concept when applied to circles.
